headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared project/filesystem workflows and unrestricted writes.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads/writes shared local files and MCP configs, while gpt-engineer writes files in a user project directory and can ingest generated content through stdin/stdout or files. That creates a plausible file-based prompt-injection bridge in default workflows, though not a guaranteed one. The pair lacks a documented provenance barrier.
conditions: IF ECC reads project files produced by gpt-engineer as instructions
IF the two agents share a writable workspace or copied prompt files
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files as prompts
Add a manual review step before ECC consumes gpt-engineer output
Use read-only mounts for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, and security findings, and gpt-engineer writes generated source code in the project directory. If they share a workspace, sensitive context from ECC can be exposed to gpt-engineer outputs or vice versa. The profiles do not show local-only inference for both, so leakage risk is more than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same project directory
IF ECC stores secrets or findings in files gpt-engineer can read
mitigations: Use separate project roots
Keep secrets out of shared directories
Restrict file permissions on ECC state files
Review generated code before copying it into ECC-managed areas
requires-engineering: isolate agent storage namespaces

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, read and write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses. ECC also modifies git state, while gpt-engineer writes files in the project directory; overlapping writes without explicit locking make destructive conflicts likely in default multi-instance use. The pair therefore has a strong write-conflict pathway.
conditions: IF both agents run against the same repository or project directory
IF git operations occur without external locking
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use separate clones or worktrees
Pause one agent before the other edits files
Commit or stash before switching agents
requires-engineering: add file-locking and coordination primitives

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer is designed to write files then offer to run, and ECC’s workflow centers on skills and MCP-driven automation. If ECC consumes gpt-engineer output as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes or downstream actions without verification. The interaction is plausible in default workflows and can propagate incorrect code or instructions.
conditions: IF ECC treats gpt-engineer output as trusted input
IF generated code is executed or committed without review
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Compare outputs against tests or linting
Disable auto-commit from either agent
Limit ECC to advisory mode for gpt-engineer artifacts
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles session summaries, hooks, agent definitions, and security findings, while gpt-engineer handles generated source code and can execute generated code with the user's privileges. If regulated data or secrets are placed into the shared project flow, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not show matching compliance controls, so mismatch risk is material.
conditions: IF regulated data is included in ECC-managed files
IF generated code or logs are retained longer than policy allows
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools
Set short retention for ECC session artifacts
Delete generated artifacts after use
Review logging settings before running either agent
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
